ranking.verdict: The only direction whose surface is not a period style, whose phone layout cannot break, and where a seventh link is invisible. It is also the least exciting, which is the correct trade for a permanent front door. Top pick.
strengths: Longevity is structural, not stylistic. Hairline-ruled type lists, flush-left masthead, grotesque-against-mono: this idiom is 60 years old, not 3. Nothing in the CSS is a 2026 gesture — no bloom, no grain, no backdrop-filter, no reveal keyframes (it has zero @keyframes at all). Compare d3, which names its own surface as 'the most-imitated look on the internet right now'.

Absorbs a seventh link with literally no design decision. `.index` is border-top plus six `.row` each with border-bottom; a seventh row adds 36.7px to a 431.7px stack and looks identical. Contrast d4, where item 7 hits `grid-auto-flow: column` against only two explicit columns and spawns an implicit third `auto` column — a visible hole in a hard-ruled frame.

Phone behaviour is the best in the set and the only one that actually reaches 44px. The `@media (max-width: 430px)` branch drops the annotation column and spends the freed height on `padding: 0.875rem 0` for a measured 44.59px row. d2 ships 30.8–32.3px rows, d5 ships 34px, d4 relies on minmax division.

A single column that cannot wrap kills the 2+1 reflow bug outright rather than replacing it with a different grid that has its own breakpoints. No container queries, no `cqw`, no boundary conditions — the two directions that use container units (d2, d3) both had a container query that silently failed or sat on a knife edge.

Both themes work, with `--ink-soft` at 6.77:1 / 7.25:1 replacing the failing `--muted` (verified: #8a8a90 is 3.12:1 on --bg-1 and 2.51:1 on --bg-2 in the shipping Base.astro). Base.astro already declares `color-scheme: light dark`; d1 honours it, d2 and d3 discard it.

Flattening the ground to `--paper` is a quietly good call that the others miss the significance of: it removes the radial-gradient whose outer stop #dcdce0 is what dragged #5b3df5 to 4.48:1. Half the accent fix is deleting the vignette.
weaknesses: The favicon relationship is asserted rather than felt. At rest, on a phone, with no hover, the entire use of --accent is one period glyph after the name. I opened public/favicon.svg: it is a #5b3df5 rounded square with a white bold `g`. d4 puts that exact object on the page; d1 puts a full stop. This is d1's thinnest seam and the one thing I would graft in.

At 0.875rem the icons stop being logos and become texture. Verified against the real assets: Strava is a two-chevron path and Venmo is an SVG `<text>` node — neither survives 14px, and `scale(1.14)`/`scale(1.06)` does not rescue identifiability, only weight. The words carry 100% of recognition, so a stranger scanning for a familiar coloured mark finds nothing to lock onto.

The mono column has a hard ~20-character ceiling (measured 178px of track against 127px for `rukna1000@gmail.com`) and it ellipsises from the right, so the one string where truncation destroys meaning — the email domain — is the one at risk. And on the phone branch that column is `display: none`, which throws away both the personality and the actual address.

Uppercase 0.115em-tracked labels plus a right-aligned mono column plus hairlines is one bad edit from reading as an API reference table. The 40px name is the only thing holding it on the right side of that line, and the direction depends on a self-hosted face it does not yet have — on Roboto, -0.038em reads cramped rather than confident.

No warmth and no image. This is a bet that confidence reads better than charm. I think it is the right bet for a front door, but a stranger expecting personality gets none until they read the annotation column.

ranking.verdict: Wins the two-second identity read outright and for a verifiable reason, then loses on the two axes that decide a permanent site: it cannot absorb a seventh link without visibly breaking, and it cannot hold a bio at all.
strengths: Best favicon coherence in the set, and it is not a claim — it is the same object. public/favicon.svg is `rect fill=#5b3df5` plus `text fill=#ffffff` bold `g`. `.mark` is `background: var(--accent)` = #5b3df5 with `.mark-glyph` = `g` at `font-weight: 800` in `--on-accent` #ffffff. Tab icon and page carry one identical mark. Nobody else does this; d1 derives a period, d3 derives a bloom.

The composition underneath is the durable part: asymmetric `grid-template-rows: minmax(7.5rem, 1.05fr) auto minmax(11rem, 1fr) auto`, ordinals as an index, mono metadata. That is Müller-Brockmann, and it would survive a complete retune of the accent.

Only direction that handles Windows High Contrast. The `@media (forced-colors: active)` block is genuinely necessary here, because `gap: 1px` over `background: var(--rule)` loses every hairline when backgrounds are forced — a structure-only design would have rendered as unstyled blocks. Nobody else noticed.

The `--ink-3-inv` token is the sharpest colour catch across all five reports: the ordinal on an inverted cell lands at exactly 3.00:1 light / 2.88:1 dark without it. And raising dark `--rule` from #48484f (2.13:1) to #62626b (3.19:1) was mandatory for a design whose only ornament is the hairline.

The Venmo fix is real and I confirmed the mechanism against the asset. index.astro line 36 sets `font-family="Georgia…" font-style="italic" font-weight="700"` as SVG presentation attributes, which lose to any author rule — so `SCOPE .c-venmo .glyph svg text { font-family: var(--sans) … }` genuinely pulls it into the display face. Every direction should steal this.
weaknesses: Cannot take a seventh link. `.links` is `grid-template-columns: 1.18fr 1fr; grid-template-rows: repeat(3, 1fr); grid-auto-flow: column`. Item 7 creates an implicit third column at `auto` width, so the whole frame goes lopsided with one item alone in a narrow trailing column — and in a design where every cell is outlined, that hole is the most visible thing on the page. Going to 2x4 instead leaves a naked empty ruled cell. Either way it is a re-derivation, not an edit.

Cannot take a bio at all. `.role` is 0.625rem uppercase mono with 0.085em tracking — it physically cannot hold a sentence — and `grid-template-areas` is locked to four rows against two `minmax()` floors. A fifth area means re-tuning 7.5rem/1.05fr and 11rem/1fr and re-checking the 25rem floor. This is the definition of collapsing under a future edit.

The spine costs 56px of a 380px phone — about 15% of the screen width — for pure ornament, while the labels it crowds are 0.625rem uppercase mono at 0.06em tracking. Ten-pixel tracked caps is the least scannable label treatment of the five, and it is the tier a stranger has to read to know where the links go.

The violet is load-bearing to the point of being a hostage. The spine is ~17% of the panel and the direction concedes it cannot be 'toned down' — if Ankur ever tires of #5b3df5, this direction has to be re-pitched rather than retuned. A permanent front door should not be that tightly coupled to one hex.
Full-cell inversion to near-white on every pointer pass in dark mode is a bright block flashing six times as you move down the page. Correct as an idea, tiring on your own site at night.
Hard-rule neobrutalism plus one saturated colour is legibly 2022–2026. Less date-stamped than d3's bloom, but it will read as a period surface well before d1's hairlines do.
`text-transform: uppercase` on the name means Chrome exposes the transformed string to the a11y tree and some screen readers spell short caps words letter by letter. Small, real, unfixable in CSS.

ranking.verdict: The best resting composition after d1 and by far the sharpest QA, wrapped in the one feature that disqualifies it from being a front door: an unskippable 900ms entrance that plays on every single load.
strengths: The at-rest page is close to d1's and durable for the same reasons: 34px name, two mono lines, one hairline, a single flex column that cannot reflow, no gradient-heavy surface.
Takes a seventh link trivially — one more `<a>` in a `flex-direction: column`, no grid arithmetic — and a bio slots under `.role` with no structural consequence. Second-best headroom in the set.

The QA found the single best bug of all five: `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` set `.label::after { opacity: 0 }` at equal specificity and later in source than the `(hover: none)` block's `{ opacity: .3 }`, so turning reduced motion ON silently deleted the touch affordance that block existed to provide. Enabling one a11y setting destroying another is exactly the class of defect nobody catches by reading.

The grid-versus-flex centring catch is expert work: an over-sized grid track resolves to the start edge, so the one mark deliberately scaled past its slot (the 25px Venmo V in a 20px box, measured dx +2.5px) was the one mark knocked off the shared left edge — plus the non-obvious follow-on that flex items default to `flex-shrink: 1` and would have clawed it back, hence `flex: none`.

Hover choreography is the most alive in the set and costs nothing at rest: mark translateX(-2px), label translateX(4px), a true 1px underline wiping via scaleX, and a radial bloom opening behind the mark.
weaknesses: Every revealed element is `animation: … both` with a delay, so the page is genuinely blank at t=0 and the last link lands at 860ms. A two-second first impression spends nearly half of itself watching furniture arrive — and there is no zero-JS way to not replay it. The direction concedes it is 'mildly tiresome the twentieth' time. On the page you and everyone who knows you loads most often, that is the definition of novelty that embarrasses you in a year.

Because the hidden states live in keyframes with fill-mode `both`, any path that loads the CSS but does not run animations leaves rows blank. Reduced motion is handled; a content blocker or print path is not. A page whose only job is routing should not have a failure mode where the routes are invisible.

The accent barely exists where the site is actually used. On a phone at rest the entire brand purple is a 2.5rem segment of `linear-gradient` hairline plus a 30%-opacity underline — so the whole justification for finally using --accent evaporates on touch. The `(hover: none)` `:active` patch is honest but it is a patch on a structural asymmetry.

`max-width: 22rem` (352px) on `.stage` means the composition is a narrow column adrift in any real viewport, and the direction admits it 'starts to look like an unfinished layout past ~1800px'. The current site's problem is that it reads unfinished; this reintroduces that at desktop width.

Lowercase brand labels (`github`, `linkedin`, `venmo`) are a datable mannerism, and 'Runs, rides, records' is a pun that only lands if you already know about the Strava and Spotify links — backwards on a page whose job is to explain who he is.

Six hand-tuned SVG sizes tied to six specific viewBoxes, with the Venmo entry depending on Georgia's cap height, and `--i:0`–`--i:10` assigned by hand in the markup. Swapping any icon or inserting a link silently desyncs something with no test to catch it.

ranking.verdict: The most beautifully executed panel here and the worst possible choice for a permanent site. It is a screenshot of 2025 that will read as one in 2028, and it says so itself.
strengths: Exceptional measurement rigour — rasterising the feTurbulence data-URI to find it contributes +4.7/255 mean and then computing every contrast pair against the grained, saturated, bloom-lit composite is work almost nobody does. The finding that `overlay` and `soft-light` collapse to ~0.4/255 on a near-black ground and only `plus-lighter` registers is a genuinely useful fact.

Real bugs caught: the `clamp(1.625rem, 6.6cqw, 2.125rem)` name sat on its 26px floor from 280px all the way to 440px — a dead fluid ramp across most of the stated range; `calc(90ms + var(--i) * 48ms)` with no fallback goes invalid at computed-value time and resets delay to 0s; `list-style: none` strips the list role in Safari.

The `@media (hover: none)` reset of exactly the three hover rules is the correct fix for the right problem — five of six tiles open a new tab, so a tapped tile comes back still holding the accent border and glow — and tokenising `--drop` so the shadow stack cannot drift in three places is genuine maintenance foresight.

Strongest atmospheric use of #5b3df5 in the set: an eight-stop bloom sited as one off-frame light source, which also justifies the tiles' `inset 0 1px 0` top-edge lip. It is internally coherent in a way decorative accents usually are not.
weaknesses: Fails my primary test on its own admission: 'reads as 2023-2026 SaaS, and it will date as a period style the way skeuomorphic gradients and long shadows did.' Bloom plus grain plus frosted tile plus staggered mask-wipe is the single most-imitated vocabulary of this moment. In three years this is the one that looks like a template.

Says 'follows design fashion', not 'has taste and technical depth'. There is no typographic idea and no structural idea — the sophistication is all in the ground treatment. The `mono` wordmark is the only technical signal and it is 0.6875rem.
A seventh link in `repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr))` leaves a visible half-empty final row. Less catastrophic than d4's implicit third column, but a 2x3 is a closed number and this design chose it.

Abandons light mode by construction, not by preference — the frosted tiles, top-edge lip, additive grain and derived accent are all functions of the near-black ground, so `data-theme="light"` gets the dark card anyway. Base.astro already declares `color-scheme: light dark`; this is a regression no token swap can patch.

The sub-labels are the weakest copy in the whole comparison. 'the code', 'work history', 'say hello', 'on repeat' — capped near 12 characters and ellipsising if lengthened, so the copy budget enforces exactly the twee register. d1's factual mono column ('rukna1000@gmail.com', 'rides & runs') does the same job without the voice problem.
Six `backdrop-filter` tiles are six compositor layers; the blur may quietly not render on low-end Android. It fails soft, but the frosted quality is the entire point, so what fails is the design.

Every contrast figure in the palette is computed with the grain peak composited in, and `--ink-3` sits at 4.64:1 at the ceiling. Any future lightening of `--ground`, any bump to grain opacity, or any fourth ink level breaks AA invisibly. That is a booby trap for whoever edits this in 2028.

ranking.verdict: Craftiest single detail in the set and the least fit for purpose. A terminal transcript is a costume rather than a composition, it forfeits light mode, and it is the one direction with nowhere to put a bio.
strengths: `--lbcol: 8.5ch` resolving against the row's own font-size is the best single technical idea across all five directions: the label column self-corrects to whatever advance width the shipped mono has, so swapping the typeface cannot desync the grid. d1's `max-content` plus fixed padding does not have this property.

Two genuinely serious layout bugs found and fixed: a container query cannot restyle its own container, so `@container { SCOPE { --px … } }` left row padding at 24px while font sizes correctly stepped down — a silently half-applied breakpoint; and `display:flex` + `justify-content:center` + `overflow:hidden` distributes negative free space upward, measured -33px at 320px with the name's ascenders sliced off and unreachable. Replacing it with `margin-block: auto` (which resolves to 0 when free space is negative) is exactly right.
Handling narrow width by dropping the path to a second line under the label — rather than hiding the column — is better than d1's `display: none`, because the information survives.
The metaphor is at least load-bearing rather than decorative: six links genuinely is the shape of one `ls`, and it stops at six without needing filler.
weaknesses: Reads as engineer-cosplay, not taste. A stranger who is not an engineer gets a wall of 13–14px monospace, and the path column actively works against the page's job: `/athletes/115751174` communicates nothing and `/user/theultimatepanda` front-loads mechanism over meaning. This is the direction most likely to feel embarrassing in a year — not because it dates, but because it is a theme.

Zero headroom for anything that is not a link. A bio or a projects section requires a second invented command and a second prompt, at which point it becomes an actual fake shell session and collapses into the kitsch it spent all its restraint avoiding. The direction names this itself.

Dark-only with no light fallback, and unpatchable: the phosphor accent, selection bar and grain are all derived from the near-black ground. A recruiter opening it on a phone in daylight gets a low-luminance page; a light-mode user gets ignored.

Worst small-screen numbers here. Rows measure 30.8–32.3px, and even after the vertical-rhythm fix the footer sits ~11px below the fold at 320px. Monospace at 13px has narrower apertures and more uniform word shapes than a good sans at the same size, and the 19-character email is where that bites.

The one accent is violet-on-black because the favicon forced it, and the direction concedes violet-on-black 'reads faintly AI startup in 2026' in a way green or amber would not. So the colour is simultaneously mandatory and off-register.

Correctness rests on two non-obvious CSS facts (container queries cannot style their own container; `ch` resolves against the using element's font-size), both discovered only by measurement. A maintainer tidying tokens back onto the container or font-size back onto the labels breaks the grid in a way that still looks plausible at desktop width.

judges.notes:
METHOD: I read the real source rather than trusting the briefs — /Users/ankur/Documents/projects/deploy-goobta.io/services/goobta.io/src/pages/index.astro, src/layouts/Base.astro, and public/favicon.svg. Two things there changed my ranking.

(1) The favicon is not abstract purple. public/favicon.svg is `<rect rx=14 fill="#5b3df5">` plus a white `font-weight=700` letter `g`. So "make --accent earn the favicon" has a much stronger answer than any direction except d4 realised: put the actual mark on the page. d4 does exactly that and it is why it wins the two-second read.

(2) The Venmo asset is `<text … font-family="Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" font-style="italic" font-weight="700">V</text>` — presentation attributes, which lose to any author rule. d4's CSS-only override therefore genuinely works, and it is not theoretical.

THE ONE GRAFT THAT MATTERS — d4's `g` onto d1. d1 is the right direction and its single weakest seam is that at rest, on a phone, with no hover, its entire use of --accent is one period glyph. That is a thin thing to hang the favicon relationship on. Take d4's move at d1's scale: set `goobta.io` in the colophon with the `g` in `--accent`, or put a small violet rounded-square `g` tile above the masthead at ~20px. It costs d1 nothing — no spine, no 56px of phone width, no layout change — and it closes the gap between tab icon and page that d1 currently only asserts. Do NOT graft d4's spine itself; the 17% violet block is what dates d4 and what makes its violet a hostage.

THREE SMALLER GRAFTS, in order of value:
— d2's `--lbcol: 8.5ch` technique onto d1's `.note`. d1's annotation column has a measured ~20-character ceiling and ellipsises from the right, so the Email row loses the domain — the only part that carries meaning. Sizing the label track in `ch` against the row's own font-size (which requires font-size on `.row`, not on the children) makes the grid self-correcting when Inter Tight / Commit Mono actually ship, which `max-content` + `padding-left: 1.5rem` does not.
— d2's narrow-width treatment onto d1's phone branch. d1 does `SCOPE .note { display: none }` at ≤430px, which deletes both the personality and the email address from the version most visitors see. d2 drops the second column to its own line under the label instead. d1 already buys the vertical room by widening rows to 44px; spend a little of it keeping the information.
— d4's `@media (forced-colors: active)` block and Venmo `<text>` override onto whatever ships. d4 is the only direction that considered Windows High Contrast at all. And the real fix for Venmo is to replace the `<text>` node with a drawn path in index.astro before launch — the CSS override is a stopgap in every direction that uses it.

WHAT I DELIBERATELY WOULD NOT GRAFT: d5's load stagger. Its hover choreography (mark −2px, label +4px, hairline underline wipe, bloom) is better than d1's 3px chevron and is worth importing wholesale, because it is pure pointer-state and costs nothing at rest. But the `animation: … both` reveal is d5's liability, not its asset: 900ms of assembly on every load of the page you open most, plus a failure mode where content stays at opacity 0 if animations never run. Import the hover, leave the entrance.

CROSS-CUTTING OBSERVATION: all five directions solve the brief's stated bug list — every one kills the drop-shadow, every one adds a real name, every one normalises the six glyphs with per-mark optical sizing, every one retires the failing `--muted` (which I confirmed at 3.12:1 on --bg-1 and 2.51:1 on --bg-2). So the listed problems are not the differentiator. The differentiator is the three things the brief actually asks about, and they sort the field cleanly: only d1 and d5 keep a working light theme (Base.astro already declares `color-scheme: light dark`, so d2 and d3 discarding it is a regression, not a stylistic choice); only d1 and d5 use a single column that cannot reflow; and only d1 and d5 absorb a seventh link without a design decision — d4's `grid-auto-flow: column` against two explicit columns spawns an implicit third column, and d3's `repeat(2, 1fr)` leaves a half-empty row. Six is a closed number and two directions built on it.

ONE HONEST CAVEAT ON MY TOP PICK: d1 is the correct choice and it is also the least memorable of the five. It wins on permanence, phone and headroom, and it loses on charm to d3 and on mark-recognition to d4. If Ankur's actual priority is a page that makes people say "nice site" rather than one he never has to touch again, d4 is the better brief-fit — but he should then accept that he is signing up to redesign it when he adds a seventh link.

ranking.verdict: The only one of the five that renders as a finished, closed object rather than a layout containing content. Wins on measurable typographic craft, not on concept novelty — and it ships one glaring uncorrected glyph that its own premise cannot afford.
strengths: Measured: indexR / rowR / markR / colophonR all resolve to 441px, and all six labelL to 56px, with nameL at 28px. Every element lands on one of exactly two vertical edges. It is the only direction whose composition closes into a rectangle instead of trailing off.
Real four-tier scale — 40 / 15 / 13 / 11px, a 3.08x display-to-label ratio. Actual hierarchy, not four sizes of sibling. Compare d2's 1.57x.

The annotation column is load-bearing composition, not garnish: the note right-aligns to the same 441px edge as the hairline, so each row is a resolved span. d4 builds the identical construct and leaves the middle empty; that is the difference between the two.
Hover promotes the row's existing bottom hairline to accent instead of introducing a new object. Verified in render — the most elegant state change in the set, and the cheapest.
Accent discipline is genuine and auditable: one use at rest (the period), one on state, one on focus. One hue, three jobs, and the purple favicon finally has a referent.
weaknesses: Does not fix the Venmo mark. Verified in render: a Georgia bold-italic V sits among five geometric glyphs. On a page whose entire argument is typographic control, this is the loudest error on the screen, and it is in the deliverable while d4 fixed the same asset in one CSS rule.

13px uppercase at 0.115em tracking + a right-aligned mono column + 1px hairlines is one edit away from an API reference table. Only the 40px masthead holds it on the right side of that line, and the direction knows it.
The index opens on --rule-strong (0.32) and closes on --rule (0.14). At this scale the unequal bracket reads as an unfinished bottom edge rather than an intentionally open one.

Name is a fixed 2.5rem. At the 560 panel it under-asserts against six full-measure rules — the six hairlines dominate by area and the masthead shrinks to a corner. The composition is genuinely stronger at 380–470 than wide.
Swiss editorial grotesque against mono metadata is the house style of engineer-designers right now. This is restraint executed well, not an idea. It will age gracefully and be forgotten.

ranking.verdict: The only entry with a real compositional idea rather than a good layout, and the only one that actually fixed the Venmo glyph. Undercut by a self-inflicted ordering error and a secondary tier with no internal hierarchy.
strengths: Genuine composition, measured: 109px of void above a bottom-flush name inside a 184.8px cell, with the 'g' at the top of a 15.3%-wide spine. That diagonal across an empty middle is negative space doing structural work — nothing else here attempts it.

The accent is committed rather than sprinkled. A flat violet field 15% of the panel wide is a decision you cannot quietly walk back, and it answers the unused-accent brief more completely than a period does.

Only direction that fixes the Venmo V in the deliverable — pulls the SVG <text> into the sans at 800 via presentation-attribute override. Verified in render: it reads as a member of the set. The other four wrote a to-do.
Hover inverts the entire cell. It is the only state change that is a graphic event rather than a decoration, and it is consistent with a design whose ornament is structure.
At 380 the composition reads most clearly of any direction — the void is legible as intent, not as leftover space.
weaknesses: Measured: ordinals in visual order are 01, 04, 02, 05, 03, 06. Numbering an index and then flowing it column-major defeats the numbering, and the ordinals are the device the direction leans on for its work/personal grouping. Either go row-major or drop the numbers.
cellWidths measure 197 vs 167px. The 1.18fr split is too subtle to read as intentional and too large to disappear — it reads as a grid that is slightly wrong.

12 separate elements at ≤11px uppercase tracked mono (role, six labels, mark-word, ordinals, year, separator). The entire secondary tier is one undifferentiated texture with no hierarchy inside it — monotonous, and the 10px tagline strip is genuinely cramped.
At 560 the cells stretch and the label-to-ordinal gap becomes a void. Same construct as d1's row, worse resolved, because nothing occupies the middle.

SF at 800 uppercase with -0.03em is the neo-brutalist default, and the whole spine gesture rests on a distinctive 'g' the system stack does not provide. The idea is renting a letterform it does not have.
Roughly seven horizontal rules plus the vertical and the spine edge. 'Structure is the only ornament' shades into 'this is a form'.

ranking.verdict: Unusually disciplined for a terminal pastiche, and its hover is the best-argued interaction here. But it fails the one job the page has — the name does not command the page — and its type system measures as a single face plus an accident.
strengths: Grid rigor is real, not claimed: all six paths start at x=169.6 and all six labels at x=88, single values. The spine holds.

The hover is the strongest state design in the set: a full-bleed selection bar that ignores the text inset, plus a marker that snaps rather than fades. This is literally how TUI selection behaves, so the metaphor pays off in interaction instead of in decoration.

Genuinely refuses the kitsch it could have reached for — no window chrome, no ASCII art, no fake whoami, no scanlines, no typing animation. The restraint is the only thing separating it from cosplay and it holds.
The metaphor is structurally honest: six links really is the shape of one ls, so it stops at six without needing filler.
weaknesses: Hierarchy failure, measured: 22px name against 14px rows is 1.57x. For a page whose entire purpose is to say a name, the name does not dominate — and at the 560 panel it reads as a line of body copy with a sigil in front of it.

Computed font families across the whole panel come back as exactly ['ui-monospace', 'Georgia']. One measurement captures both problems: there is no type contrast anywhere, and the single non-mono thing on the page is the uncorrected Georgia italic Venmo V — maximally conspicuous inside a strict monospace grid.
The path column is mechanism dressed as information. '/athletes/115751174' and '/user/theultimatepanda' communicate nothing to a reader and occupy the widest column on the page.
Violet phosphor on near-black is the 2026 AI-startup default. The direction admits green or amber would read less trend-bound, which concedes the point.
Commits to dark with no light path, and at 560 the listing's hairlines span the full measure while content stops well short — dead right field.

ranking.verdict: Contains the single most elegant detail in the set and the least resolved composition. It is d1 with the load-bearing elements deleted, betting everything on motion that the render shows to be a 6px event.
strengths: The hairline with a 2.5rem accent lead-in is the best small idea in the whole set: one line carrying the brand color as an inflection rather than as an applied decoration. Worth stealing.
The counter-drift on hover — icon -2px, label +4px — is a genuinely considered decision. Most people would move both the same direction.
Cleanest, quietest ground of the five; the near-flat gradient (bg-1 to bg-2 only ~3% apart) is correctly judged.
weaknesses: Measured compositional failure: the rule spans 352px (l=59 to r=411) while the widest link's right edge is 160px. 251px — 71% of the measure the rule establishes — is empty. The rule promises a column the layout never uses, so it reads as a line to nowhere. At 560 it compounds: a 352px slab centered in a 560px panel, with dead space both inside and outside the slab.
At rest the accent is a 40px segment of a single 1px hairline — about 11% of one line. Of all five directions claiming to give the favicon a reason to exist, this one gives it the least.

The six rows carry no structure whatsoever: no rules, no notes, no ordinals, no numbering. This is d1's construct with everything that made d1 cohere removed, which is why nothing establishes a right edge.

The entire thesis is deferred to a ~900ms load stagger and the hover. Forced-hover render confirms the visible result is 'the link underlines and nudges' — an ordinary outcome for a design with no second idea underneath it.

Lowercase mono brand names repeat d2's move without d2's justifying metaphor. And the stage is margin-inline:auto centered while left-aligned internally, so the block floats with no relationship to the panel edges.

ranking.verdict: Competently built pastiche. This is precisely the look the brief warned against, executed without a single decision that could not have been generated by anyone else, and its hierarchy is inverted: the decoration is louder than the identity.
strengths: Technically the most careful build: the 8-stop bloom genuinely avoids the hard-edged blob a 3-stop gradient gives you, the grain contribution was measured rather than guessed, and the per-mark optical sizing works in render.
The only direction with any softness or warmth, which is a real axis the others abandon entirely.
weaknesses: This is the template. Computed style confirms the full 2023–26 dark-SaaS kit unmodified: 12px radius, hairline border, inset top lip, backdrop-filter blur(6px) saturate(1.35), 2x3 card grid, tiny glowing dot, mono wordmark, corner bloom, noise overlay. Nothing here is specific to this person or this site.

Inverted hierarchy, measured: the name is 30.8px — second-smallest display size in the set — while a full-panel violet gradient is the loudest element on screen. The decoration outranks the identity on a page whose only job is identity.

The lede's box sits at y=123–165, squarely inside the bloom's hot zone. The most decorated region of the page is where the text is forced to live, and the direction's own contrast math has to account for it.
Weakest copy in the set: 'the code', 'say hello', 'on repeat'. 'say hello' is indistinguishable from placeholder.
Six labelled tiles in a 2x3 grid reads as a SaaS feature grid. Swap the strings and it is any product page — the exact opposite of a personal site with taste.
Commits to dark with no light path, for a vocabulary that is dark-only by construction, so there is no cheap way back if that turns out to matter.

judges.notes:
METHOD — I did not judge from the write-ups. I rebuilt all five verbatim with the real production SVGs from src/pages/index.astro, rendered them side by side at 380/470/560 in both themes, forced one row per direction into its hover state (rewriting ':hover' to a class, since hover cannot be screenshotted), and measured geometry from the live layout. Harness: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ankur-Documents-projects-deploy-goobta-io/768730c8-a64f-487a-8025-05902b2eb16a/scratchpad/crit/ (build.py, build_hover.py, d1–d5.html/.css, grid-*.html, hover-*.html). Several claims in the directions' own prose did not survive measurement; the specific numbers in each entry above are from the render, not from the pitch.

GRAFTS WORTH MAKING, in value order:

1. d4's Venmo fix onto d1 (and d2, d3, d5). d4 is the only direction that solved this, in one rule: `.c-venmo .glyph svg text { font-family: var(--sans); font-style: normal; font-weight: 800 }`. The production asset draws its V as an SVG <text> with font-family as a *presentation attribute*, which loses to any author rule — so the serif italic is fixable from CSS with no new asset. Confirmed in render: d4's V reads as a member of the set; every other direction ships a Georgia bold-italic V among five geometric marks. For d1 specifically this is not cosmetic — a page whose whole argument is typographic control cannot ship the one glyph that contradicts it. Highest value, lowest cost graft available.

2. d5's accent lead-in onto d1's opening rule. d5's best detail is `linear-gradient(90deg, accent 0 2.5rem, rule 2.5rem 100%)` on a 1px line. Applied to d1's `.index` border-top it fixes two things at once: d1 currently opens on --rule-strong and closes on --rule, an unequal bracket that reads as an unfinished bottom edge, and applying an accent inflection makes the top edge *deliberately different in kind* rather than merely heavier. It also gives d1 a second at-rest use of the accent, since right now the whole color story at rest is one period — which in dark (#a99bff) is nearly invisible at 40px.

3. d4's void-as-structure onto d1's wide end. d1's only real proportional weakness is that a fixed 2.5rem name under-asserts at 560 against six full-measure hairlines. d4 demonstrates (measured: 109px of void above a bottom-flush name) that a large deliberate void reads as composition rather than emptiness. Letting d1's name clamp up and sit lower in a taller masthead is the fix, and d1's own idealTypeface note already argues for a clamp.

4. Reverse direction, for the record: d1's annotation column is exactly what d4's cells are missing. At 560 d4's cells have a label at left, an ordinal at right, and a void between — same construct as d1's row, worse resolved. If d4 were the pick, it should adopt the note column.

5. d4 must go row-major or drop the ordinals. Measured visual order is 01, 04, 02, 05, 03, 06. This is not a taste call; it is a numbered index that defeats its own numbering, and the ordinals are the device the direction relies on for its work/personal grouping.

CROSS-CUTTING OBSERVATION — three of the five (d2, d3, d5) hide a weak or absent composition behind a surface treatment (phosphor, bloom+grain, motion). The two that scored highest (d1, d4) are the two that would still read as designed objects printed in one flat color with no interaction at all. That is the test I applied throughout, and it separates the set cleanly. Also worth flagging to whoever assembles the final: d3 and d5 both leave the brief's stated problem #2 (the unused accent) effectively unsolved — d3 by drowning it in a full-panel wash so it stops being an accent, d5 by reducing it to 11% of one hairline at rest.

ranking.verdict: The cleanest, most idiomatic CSS in the set and the most robust by default, because it wins by not spending: zero animation, zero url(), zero backdrop-filter, zero container queries, six tokens that map 1:1 onto Base.astro's existing --bg/--fg/--muted/--accent shape. Two real layout bugs, both one-liners. Its weakness is conceptual, not technical: it answers the accent/favicon brief least of any direction.
strengths: Zero motion at load. Nothing is gated behind an animation, so there is no fill-mode, no stagger, no reveal, and nothing that can fail to appear. Of the five this is the only direction where 'what if animations never run' is not even a question.
Best rem-scaling behaviour of the type-led directions: at html{font-size:32px} in a 390px box the name wraps to two lines, the deck reflows, rows and hairlines scale, nothing truncates. Verified.
Measured 44.6px rows at 320px with .note correctly display:none — a real 44px target, and the height is honestly paid for by dropping the annotation column rather than asserted.

Cleanest token layer of the five: 6 flat tokens replacing --bg-1/--bg-2/--fg/--muted/--accent one-for-one, with the radial gradient removed so every ratio is computed against a single flat ground instead of two gradient stops.
Only direction that puts 'Opens in a new tab' into the accessible name (.vh with clip-path: inset(50%), the modern correct pattern). Its a11y is genuine, not decorative.
Full-width row hit areas — measured 488px wide at desktop, so the click target is the whole line, not the label.
<article> wrapper to stop <header>/<footer> becoming document-scoped banner/contentinfo landmarks. Small, correct, and almost always missed.
weaknesses: At html{font-size:32px} the colophon spills 64px outside its container and forces a document horizontal scrollbar: .colophon box is 293px, needs 413px, .copy's right edge lands at 464 vs a container right of 400. Cause is precisely the QA-added `white-space: nowrap` on .site/.copy, which converted a graceful wrap into an overflow. `flex-wrap: wrap` fixes it.

No horizontal centering. .page is `flex:1; max-width:34rem` inside a `display:flex` SCOPE with no justify-content and no margin-inline:auto, so at any viewport wider than 544px the whole composition pins to the left edge — confirmed by screenshot at 2056px. One-line fix, but it is the default state on every desktop.

Six independent `max-content` label tracks (47.5–73.1px) because every .row is its own grid container. It only looks flush because .note is right-aligned in a minmax(0,1fr) track. This is the textbook subgrid case and subgrid is fully available in 2026; the QA notes the fragility and declines the idiom.

Weakest execution of the brief's accent problem. The accent is a period, a hover hairline and a focus ring — and it is not even the favicon's #5b3df5, having been retuned to #4b31d9. On touch, with no hover, the entire brand colour on the page is one full stop.
Hides the email address at <=430px — the single most useful string, on the most common device.
Leaves the Georgia italic Venmo V foreign among five solid marks; normalises size (0.94–1.14 scale) but not typeface. Visible in the 470px render.
No forced-colors handling; survives Windows HCM by luck rather than design.

My recomputation of its headline ratios does not reproduce its own corrections: --accent on paper is 6.98:1 (it 'corrected' 6.97 to 7.02) and --ink is 16.34:1 (claimed 16.53). All pass AA comfortably, so this is a credibility issue for a direction whose pitch is measured precision, not a shipping issue.

ranking.verdict: Structurally the best-behaved layout of the five — the only one that actually centres itself at desktop — and the ch-based grid is genuinely elegant. Held back by three self-inflicted costs: a perpetual animation, the weakest focus ring in the set, and container queries on the layout root whose documented footgun is designed in rather than designed out.
strengths: The only direction correctly centred at a large viewport: measured term centre 1028 against viewport centre 1028 at 2056px. margin-block:auto over justify-content:center is the right call and provably cannot clip content upward when free space goes negative.

--lbcol: 8.5ch resolving against .row's own font-size is the sharpest single idea in the set: the label track self-corrects to whatever mono actually ships, so swapping the typeface cannot desync the grid.
Measured 47px touch targets at 320px via the stacked <=360px branch, and zero horizontal overflow at 320px.

Grain as SCOPE::before at z-index:-1 inside isolation:isolate is the correct layering — over the gradient, under the text — and the 0.03 opacity is justified by an actual rasterised measurement of the turbulence rather than a guess.

Honest QA that found a real bug most people would miss: a container query cannot restyle its own container, so half the narrow breakpoint was silently dead. Correctly diagnosed and correctly relocated to .term.
Zero overflow at 2x root font size — the 4-column grid degrades by ellipsis rather than by breaking.
weaknesses: At html{font-size:32px} all six .hd paths truncate, including rukna1000@gmail.com. The email address — the one string a reader might need to copy — becomes unreadable for exactly the low-vision users who raised the font size.

The blinking caret is an infinite animation (d2-caret 1.1s step-end infinite). It is the only perpetual compositor animation of the five, so the page never goes idle on a static personal site. It also implies you can type where there is no input.

Weakest focus indicator in the set: `outline: 1px dashed` at -4px inset. It is perceivable because it stacks with the fill, marker and colour change, but 1px dashed is the thinnest ring here by a factor of two.

Container queries on the layout root are over-engineering once SCOPE becomes main on a full-width page — a plain @media would do. Worse, the resulting 'do not move the tokens back onto the container' hazard is documented in a comment rather than removed, which is a maintenance liability by construction.

The icon cell has 1px of headroom (16px Venmo svg in a 17px --iconcol) and centres with `display:grid; place-items:center`. I proved that construct aligns an over-sized item to the START edge, not the centre (grid offset 0,0 vs flex -2.5,-2.5). One bump to that value silently breaks the single shared x-axis the whole design is built on, and it will still look fine at desktop width.

Commits to dark but never sets `color-scheme: dark`, while Base.astro declares `color-scheme: light dark`. Scrollbars and any UA chrome follow the OS, so a light-mode OS gets a light scrollbar against near-black — and the design ignores light-preference users entirely.

aria-label="Strava, strava.com/athletes/115751174" makes a screen reader read nine digits aloud, and the aria-label overrides rather than supplements, so the 'opens in a new tab' affordance d1 provides is absent.
Serif italic Venmo V normalised by size only.

ranking.verdict: The best token architecture and the best text-scaling behaviour of all five, wrapped around a payload of decorative cost that does nothing. Its color-mix-derived surface system is the most maintainable thing in the set — and it ironically makes the light theme the direction refuses to ship nearly free.
strengths: Best rem-scaling behaviour measured: at html{font-size:32px} in 390px, zero overflow and zero truncation — the only direction with both. min-width:0 discipline on every flex/grid child plus max-width:30ch on the lede absorbs it.

Best token architecture: six translucent surfaces (--hair/--fill/--fill-hi/--lip/--lip-hi) all derived from --ink via color-mix(in oklab, …). One hue source; change --ink and every surface follows. Nothing else here is that DRY.
role="list" alongside list-style:none for the Safari/VoiceOver list-role bug — correct, necessary, and almost never done.

@media (hover: none) resetting exactly the three hover rules while leaving :focus-visible intact. Five of six links open a new tab, so a tapped tile is on screen when the user returns; only d3 and d5 handle this.
--drop tokenised so the ambient shadow appears once and is referenced three times, specifically to stop a future editor drifting one copy into a second glow.
fill-mode: backwards verified safe — with animation forced to none, every element reads opacity 1 and mask none. Content is never left hidden.
Measured 49.5px touch targets at 320px.
Grain claims are measured rather than asserted, and the plus-lighter → normal fallback genuinely lands within 1/255 on this ground.
weaknesses: No outer measure cap. .stage has no max-width and neither do .name/.lede/.head — only .nav is capped at 34rem. Screenshot at 2056px: the whole composition hugs the far left in a 544px column with ~1500px of dead field, and because the bloom is anchored at 14%/-8% it lights the EMPTY region while the content sits in the dark. The light source and the content are anti-correlated at desktop aspect.

Six backdrop-filter: blur(6px) tiles that blur nothing. The grain is painted ABOVE the tiles at z-index:3, so each tile's backdrop is flat ground plus a smooth 8-stop radial — zero high-frequency content. Only saturate(135%) has any effect. That is six compositor layers and a per-paint readback for a visual no-op, and the QA's own 'the tiles still read correctly if blur doesn't render' admission proves it is inessential.
~1034ms of staggered reveal before content is fully present, on a page whose entire job is routing to six links. d1 and d4 cost 0ms.

The d3-wipe keyframes duplicate eight mask longhands across both from and to (16 declarations, half of them -webkit- prefixes Safari has not needed since 15.4) with a comment forbidding refactoring. The clean fix — put the mask on a wrapper so it never touches the element carrying the shadow and outline — is available and not taken.
Commits to dark with no `color-scheme: dark` despite Base.astro declaring `light dark`, and despite an architecture that would make a light theme nearly free by flipping two tokens.
Nine inline style="--i:N" attributes put presentation in the markup, and the stagger index has to be hand-maintained.
font-weight: 550 resolves to a real 550 only on variable faces; it snaps unpredictably on static Segoe UI, i.e. on much of the audience.
Serif italic Venmo V normalised by size only.

ranking.verdict: The best ideas in the set sitting on the least robust implementation. It is the only direction that actually fixes the Venmo mark, actually uses the favicon colour, and actually handles Windows High Contrast — and it is also the only direction that destroys its own content at a 2x user font size. Its accessibility is half genuine, half decorative: it handles the rare adaptation and fails the common one.
strengths: The only direction that genuinely fixes the Venmo mark instead of enlarging the serif V. SVG presentation attributes lose to author CSS, so `.c-venmo .glyph svg text { font-family: var(--sans); font-style: normal }` pulls it into the display face — and it deliberately leaves font-size alone so the asset's own centring survives. I confirmed visually in the 470px render that d4's V is upright and sans while d1, d2, d3 and d5 all still show Georgia italic. This is the brief's 'nothing normalizes them', actually answered.

Strongest answer to the unused-accent/orphaned-favicon problem by a wide margin: the literal favicon hex #5b3df5 at full saturation across a whole vertical band, plus a full-cell accent fill on focus. Every other direction either retunes the hue away from the favicon or confines it to hover states.
Best focus state of the five: the accent claims the entire cell plus an inset 2px white ring. Unmistakable, high contrast, and clearly distinct from hover.

The only direction handling @media (forced-colors: active) — and it is necessary, not decorative: the `gap:1px over background` technique loses every hairline when backgrounds are forced, so a structure-is-the-ornament design would render as unstyled blocks. Correct diagnosis, correct fix, no layout shift under border-box.
--ink-3-inv is real second-order contrast work: without it the ordinal inside an inverted cell lands at exactly 3.00:1. Almost nobody checks the de-emphasised tier against the inverted ground.
Correctly raised dark --rule from #48484f (2.13:1) to #62626b (3.19:1) on the grounds that those hairlines delimit interactive cells and are therefore governed by 1.4.11 rather than exempt.
Zero animation anywhere, so there is nothing to disable and nothing that can fail to appear.
Largest touch targets measured: 73px at 320px. Spine verified reaching the frame bottom with a 1px gap at 2056px, so the corner-to-corner fix is real.
weaknesses: At html{font-size:32px} the design destroys its own content. Measured: .name at 64px in a 202px cell, 'ANKUR' needs 213px and has 146px, 'GUPTA' needs 203px and has 146px — the name renders as 'ANKU▌GUPT▌', sliced by overflow:hidden. Worse, all six .label elements collapse to clientWidth 0 while needing 66–106px, so the page becomes six unidentifiable icons plus ordinals. Root cause is the fixed 4.5rem spine plus the 2rem clamp floor, and the two QA-added 'hardening' edits (overflow:hidden on .name, min-width:0/overflow:hidden on .label) are exactly what convert overflow into silent content destruction. This is the most common low-vision adaptation there is, and it is the failure mode in the direction with otherwise the most genuine a11y work.

At desktop proportions the composition collapses. No max-width on .frame, 10cqi maxes out at 3rem, and labels/glyphs/ordinals are fixed px. Measured at 2056x1147: name cell 1953x536 with 438px of dead space above 48px type; six link cells at 1057x170px each holding a 20px glyph and an 11px label, an ink fill of roughly 0.2%. Unlike d1's and d3's missing-centering (a one-line fix) this needs a max-width AND a type ramp AND row caps — the fixed-proportion grid is the concept.
Its QA tested 380–620px panels only and never opened a desktop viewport or raised the font size, which is precisely where both failures above live.

Sticky hover on touch, and it is the most violent instance in the set: hover is a full cell inversion to near-white in dark mode, five of six links open new tabs, and there is no @media (hover: none) reset — so the tapped cell stays a bright white block when the user comes back.

Nested `1.18fr 1fr` grids with gap:1px guarantee fractional track boundaries at nearly every width. That is the highest fractional-DPR hairline-consistency exposure of the five, in the direction whose entire ornament is hairline evenness — and Chrome, Firefox and Safari round it differently.
text-transform: uppercase on the name means Chrome exposes the transformed string to the accessibility tree; some AT spells short all-caps words out letter by letter.
The 10px mono metadata tier passes at 5.75:1 but is at the small end of comfortable, and it is the first thing to feel cramped — which compounds the font-size failure above.

ranking.verdict: The sharpest engineering judgment in the set at the level of individual details — I independently verified all three of its non-obvious catches and all three are correct — attached to the worst maintainability property: correctness that depends on the source order of same-specificity rules across four interacting media blocks. It also owns the only outright touch-target failure and the most fragile focus ring.
strengths: Best-reasoned optical normalisation of the five, and the only one that noticed the email icon is viewBox 0 0 512 512 with a 4:3 glyph, not a square. It then does real ink-area math: 19x14.25x~0.85 ≈ 230px² against the GitHub disc's π×8.5² = 227px². d1, d2 and d3 all treat that asset as 1:1 and get the correction direction wrong as a result.

The grid-to-flex catch is real and I verified it independently in a clean test: place-items:center on a 20px box with a 25px child yields offset (0,0) — start-aligned — while flex align/justify-center yields (-2.5,-2.5). Confirmed again in the ported page (slot x=852 w=20, svg x=850 w=25). The `flex: none` follow-up, needed because flex-shrink would have clawed the 25px back to 20px, is a correct second-order catch that most reviewers would miss.

The @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) and (hover: hover) gate is genuine accessibility engineering: without the hover:hover qualifier, enabling reduced motion silently deleted the resting-underline affordance that the hover:none block exists to provide. One a11y setting was destroying another. Subtle, real, correctly fixed.
Correctly centred at 2056px (stage centre 1028 = viewport centre 1028) with the footer aligned to the stage's left edge.
Zero overflow and zero truncation at html{font-size:32px} — second-best scaling behaviour in the set, because a single column with width:fit-content absorbs rem growth.
@media (hover: none) gives :active the bloom and the label step so the four-part choreography survives on touch, and reduced-motion neutralises the transforms again.
Animations forced off verified clean: every .rise, .rule, .link and .foot reads opacity 1, transform none.
weaknesses: The only direction failing the touch-target comfort target: measured 34px rows at 320px, against 44.6 / 47 / 49.5 / 73 for the others. It clears the 24px 2.5.8 floor and nothing else.

Focus ring clears the next row's icon by 2px, not the 4.0px its QA reports, and overlaps the next row's box by 5px (34px flush rows, outline-offset:3px, 2px stroke, zero gap). It is the tightest ring in the set and a mono fallback with a taller line-height eats the margin entirely.

Correctness rests on the source order of equal-specificity rules across four interacting media blocks — hover:none, reduced-motion, reduced-motion+hover:hover, and max-width:430. The QA found exactly one cascade bug of that shape; the architecture will keep producing them, and a future editor reordering blocks breaks it invisibly. This is the biggest maintenance liability of the five.

The risk list argues about 'the 4rem top of its clamp' for the name, but there is no clamp — .name is a flat 2.125rem with a 1.75rem narrow override. The documentation describes code that does not exist, which undercuts the direction's own account of how it scales.

Most under-scaled composition at desktop: a 352px column (max-width:22rem) with a 34px name in a 2056px viewport. It fails gracefully, unlike d3's left-pinned block or d4's inflating cells, but it reads as small rather than restrained.

Emptiest at rest of the five — visible in the 470px comparison render. The accent is a 40px hairline segment, and on touch six permanently visible 30%-opacity underlines at roughly 1.9:1. The whole page rests on one hover interaction with no ornament, texture or second idea underneath it.
Serif italic Venmo V, normalised by size only — and its own risk list concedes the mark depends on Georgia's cap height being available.

judges.notes:
GRAFTS WORTH TAKING, highest value first.

1. d4's Venmo fix belongs in whichever direction ships. It is three lines and it is the only real answer to the brief's 'nothing normalizes them': `.c-venmo .glyph svg text { font-family: var(--sans); font-style: normal; font-weight: 700 }`. The asset at src/pages/index.astro:36 sets font-family/style/weight as SVG presentation attributes, which lose to any author rule — I confirmed the mechanism and confirmed visually that d4's V renders upright/sans while d1, d2, d3 and d5 all still show Georgia italic. Keep font-size untouched so the asset's own centring survives. Every other direction only makes the serif V bigger, which makes the mismatch more conspicuous, not less.

2. d4's @media (forced-colors: active) block. Nobody else has one. Any direction using `gap:1px over a background` for hairlines loses all of them in Windows High Contrast; d1's border-based hairlines survive but its accent period does not.

3. d3's @media (hover: none) sticky-hover reset → d1, d2 and especially d4. Five of six links open a new tab, so the tapped element is still on screen when the user returns. d4 needs this most: its hover is a full cell inversion to near-white in dark mode.

4. d5's viewBox-aware optical sizing → d1, d2, d3. All three size the email icon as if it were square; it is a 4:3 glyph in a 512-square viewBox, so at width==height it renders N wide by 0.75N tall with a full-bleed slab of ink. d5 is the only one that did the ink-area math, and d1's 0.97 scale actually makes the envelope lighter than the GitHub disc it is being normalised against.

5. d4's --ink-3-inv pattern → anything with an inverting or filled state. Checking the de-emphasised tier against the inverted ground (it lands at exactly 3.00:1 without the token) is the kind of second-order check almost everyone skips.

6. d1's .vh 'Opens in a new tab' → all. d1 is the only direction that puts it in the accessible name; d2 replaces it with an aria-label that makes AT read nine digits.

FIXES d1 NEEDS BEFORE SHIP (both one-liners, both verified):
- `.colophon { flex-wrap: wrap }` and drop the QA-added `white-space: nowrap` on .site/.copy. At html{font-size:32px} the copyright spills 64px outside the container and forces a document horizontal scrollbar. The nowrap was added to protect the vertical rhythm and it traded a graceful wrap for a WCAG 1.4.10 failure.
- `margin-inline: auto` on .page (or justify-content:center on SCOPE). Today it pins to the left edge at any viewport wider than 544px.
- Consider subgrid on .index so the six label tracks actually share a grid instead of six independent max-content tracks that only look flush because .note is right-aligned.

CROSS-CUTTING OBSERVATIONS:

Every one of the five QA passes tested only 380–620px panels. None opened a desktop viewport and none raised the root font size. Those two untested axes are where three directions fail, and they are not exotic: a desktop monitor is the modal case for this site, and enlarging text is the most common low-vision adaptation. d4 fails both catastrophically; d3 fails the first; d1 fails a mild version of the second.

A pattern worth naming: in three directions, a QA-added 'hardening' edit is the direct cause of the worst failure. d1's `white-space: nowrap` turns a wrap into an overflow. d4's `overflow:hidden` on .name and `min-width:0; overflow:hidden` on .label turn overflow into silent destruction of the person's name and all six labels. Clipping is not hardening — it converts a visible, fixable symptom into invisible data loss.

Reported contrast ratios should not be trusted to two decimals. Recomputing d1's with the standard sRGB relative-luminance formula gives --accent 6.98:1 (its QA 'corrected' the author's 6.97 to 7.02, moving in the wrong direction) and --ink 16.34:1 versus a claimed 16.53. Everything still passes AA comfortably, so nothing needs repalette-ing — but the false precision is worth stripping from any copy that reaches the client.

Two porting facts that affect all five: Base.astro already ships `* { box-sizing: border-box }`, so d1's eleven-selector enumerated box-sizing list is dead code on the real site; and there is no data-theme toggle anywhere (no JS at all), so the `:root[data-theme=...] SCOPE` blocks in d1, d4 and d5 are preview scaffolding — three duplicated token sets that must collapse to one prefers-color-scheme query on port, or they will drift. Separately, d2 and d3 both commit to dark without declaring `color-scheme: dark` while Base.astro declares `light dark`, so UA scrollbars will follow the OS and render light against near-black.

Finally, on the accent brief specifically: d4 is the clear winner and d1 the clear loser, which cuts against my ranking. d4 uses the literal favicon hex at full saturation across a large field; d1 retunes the hue to #4b31d9 and spends it on a period, a hover hairline and a focus ring — meaning on a phone, where there is no hover, the entire brand colour is one full stop. If the accent/favicon relationship matters more to the client than robustness does, d1 needs a bigger accent gesture grafted in, and the cheapest one is d4's: give the accent an actual area to occupy rather than three hairline-scale touches.
